title: Model Diagnostics
text:
Prior Sensitivity
The half-normal(0, 0.50) prior on τ was chosen based on plausible heterogeneity in transplant outcomes. The prior places 95% of its mass below τ = 0.98, which corresponds to a range of study-level ORs spanning roughly 0.14 to 7.1 around the pooled estimate — generous for transplant outcomes.
For the PTCy coefficient, the Normal(0, 0.82) prior corresponds to 95% prior mass between OR 0.20 and 5.0, ensuring the prior does not materially constrain the posterior in any outcome.






TipAssessing Prior Influence



The Bayesian τ estimates are most informative for outcomes with k ≥ 15 (OS, CMV in C1). For sparse outcomes (BSI k=6, NRM C2 k=5), the prior provides meaningful regularisation — this is a feature, not a bug, as it prevents extreme heterogeneity estimates that would arise from fitting random-effects models to very small corpora.

title: Methods
text:
This is a systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis of studies comparing post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) to alternative GVHD prophylaxis regimens in allogeneic haematopoietic cell transplantation. The extraction database comprises 251 studies (525 arms, 14 RCTs) drawn from 9 extraction blocks, with 214 papers excluded per PRISMA criteria. Two pre-specified comparisons were analysed:

Comparison 1: PTCy vs CNI+MTX/MMF-based prophylaxis
Comparison 2: PTCy vs ATG-based prophylaxis
Comparison 3: Within-PTCy dose/schedule variants (new in Block 9 expansion)

title: Methods
text:
Statistical Framework

Bayesian Random-Effects Models
All models were fit using brms with the rstan backend. The general form:
\[
\text{events}_i \mid \text{trials}_i \sim \text{Binomial}(\pi_i)
\] \[
\text{logit}(\pi_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{PTCy}_i + \beta_2 \cdot \text{tp\_early}_i + u_{j[i]}
\] \[
u_j \sim \text{Normal}(0, \tau)
\]


Prior Specification








Parameter
Prior
Rationale




\[\beta_{\text{PTCy}}\]
Normal(0, 0.82)
Weakly informative; 95% prior mass covers OR 0.20–5.0


\[\beta_{\text{tp\_early}}\]
Normal(0, 0.50)
Timepoint adjustment; modest range


Intercept
Normal(0, 1.50)
Baseline event rate


\[\tau\]
Half-Normal(0, 0.50)
Heterogeneity; calibrated to plausible variation in transplant outcomes





Model Hierarchy

M1 (Direct effect): PTCy + timepoint adjustment + random study intercept
M2 (Steroid-adjusted): M1 + arm-level systemic steroid exposure (% receiving steroids for GVHD). Missing steroid data handled via mi() (Bayesian multiple imputation within brms) where needed.
M3 (aGVHD-adjusted, CMV only): M1 + arm-level aGVHD grade II–IV cumulative incidence



MCMC Configuration

4 chains × 4,000 iterations (1,000 warmup + 3,000 sampling) = 12,000 posterior draws
Convergence assessed via R̂ (all ≤ 1.005) and effective sample sizes (bulk ESS, tail ESS)
No divergent transitions in any fitted model



Frequentist Comparison
All Bayesian models were cross-checked with frequentist random-effects models (REML) via metafor (v5.0-1) using log-OR as the effect size. BSI in Comparison 2 (k = 3) was pooled using Mantel-Haenszel fixed-effect estimation.

title: Methods
text:
Arm Classification

Comparison 1
Arms were classified as PTCy if ptcy_used == "Y" and as control if the primary prophylaxis was CNI+MTX or CNI+MMF without PTCy.


Comparison 2

Primary analysis: Clean binary — PTCy-only (ptcy_used == "Y", atg_used == "N") vs ATG-only (ptcy_used == "N", atg_used == "Y")
Sensitivity analysis: PTCy+ATG combination arms reclassified as PTCy-side; mixed-ATG arms classified by PTCy co-administration; “neither” arms excluded

title: Methods
text:
GRADE Assessment
Certainty of evidence was assessed per the GRADE Handbook (Schünemann et al.) adapted for Bayesian meta-analyses of observational studies. Starting certainty: LOW. Cross-comparison coherence was considered as a potential upgrade criterion where applicable.

title: Post-Transplant Cyclophosphamide Meta-Analysis
text:
Background. Post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) has become widely adopted for GVHD prophylaxis in allogeneic haematopoietic cell transplantation, yet comprehensive quantitative evidence synthesis across survival, GVHD, and infection outcomes — and across comparator regimens — has been lacking.
Methods. We conducted a Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis of 251 studies (14 RCTs) comparing PTCy to (1) CNI+MTX/MMF-based regimens (Comparison 1) and (2) ATG-based regimens (Comparison 2). Primary outcomes included overall survival (OS), non-relapse mortality (NRM), acute GVHD grade II–IV, CMV reactivation, bloodstream infection (BSI), and invasive fungal infection (IFI). Steroid-mediation models (M2) tested whether GVHD-driven steroid exposure confounded observed effects.
Results. PTCy was associated with improved OS (C1: OR 0.79 [0.73–0.85]; C2: OR 0.81 [0.74–0.90]) and reduced aGVHD (C1: OR 0.67; C2: OR 0.58) across both comparators. NRM benefit was substantially or completely mediated by steroid exposure in both comparisons. CMV reactivation showed a direction reversal: increased with PTCy vs CNI+MTX/MMF (OR 1.26 [1.07–1.47]) but decreased vs ATG (OR 0.92 [0.73–1.15]), consistent with a T-cell depletion depth hierarchy. BSI risk was elevated in both comparisons (C1: OR 1.87; C2: MH OR 2.03).
Conclusions. PTCy provides consistent survival and GVHD advantages regardless of comparator. The CMV direction reversal establishes that infection risk is determined by the relative depth of T-cell depletion, not by any intrinsic PTCy property. NRM benefit is steroid-mediated. GRADE certainty is LOW for OS and aGVHD, VERY LOW for other outcomes.

Figure 1: Bayesian meta-analysis — PTCy effect across outcomes and comparators. Filled circles represent direct-effect models (M1); open circles represent steroid-adjusted models (M2). The dashed vertical line marks OR = 1 (no effect). OR < 1 favours PTCy for all outcomes.






Key Findings

1. Survival and GVHD benefit. PTCy was associated with reduced overall mortality and acute GVHD in both Comparison 1 (vs CNI+MTX/MMF) and Comparison 2 (vs ATG). The effect was consistent in magnitude and direction across comparators.


2. NRM is steroid-mediated. The apparent NRM benefit was substantially or completely attenuated after adjusting for GVHD-driven steroid exposure in both comparisons, indicating that PTCy reduces NRM indirectly — through fewer GVHD episodes and less corticosteroid toxicity.


3. CMV direction reversal. PTCy increased CMV reactivation vs CNI+MTX/MMF (OR 1.26) but decreased it vs ATG (OR 0.92). This reversal confirms that CMV risk is ordered by the depth of T-cell depletion (CNI < PTCy < ATG), not by any intrinsic PTCy property.


4. BSI elevated in both comparisons. Bloodstream infection risk was approximately doubled with PTCy regardless of comparator (C1: OR 1.87; C2: MH OR 2.03), though the C2 estimate is based on only 3 studies with heterogeneous definitions.

Mechanistic Framework
The findings resolve into a unified framework built on two separable consequences of PTCy:

GVHD suppression pathway (intended): PTCy → reduced aGVHD → less steroid exposure → lower NRM → improved OS. The NRM benefit is fully steroid-mediated; the OS benefit is only partially mediated, suggesting an additional direct contribution.
T-cell lymphodepletion pathway (unintended): PTCy depletes CMV-specific and bacterial-specific T cells during engraftment. The CMV direction reversal across comparisons confirms this is a depth-of-depletion effect rather than a PTCy-specific one.

title: Discussion
text:
The totality of findings across six pre-specified outcomes and two independent comparisons informs a mechanistic framework built on the distinction between two immunological consequences of PTCy.


PTCy eliminates alloreactive T cells during the critical window of allorecognition, reducing acute GVHD grade II–IV across both comparisons. This propagates downstream:

NRM benefit shows steroid mediation in both comparisons
OS benefit is only partially mediated, suggesting an additional direct contribution — most plausibly graft-versus-leukaemia preservation




The same cyclophosphamide pulse depletes the nascent CMV- and bacterial-specific T-cell repertoire. This manifests as elevated infection risk — but the magnitude and direction depend on the comparator’s own depletion depth.

section: CMV: Evidence for the Depletion Hierarchy
text:
CMV: Evidence for the Depletion Hierarchy

Primary analysis
C1 CMV remains consistently harmful: PTCy increases CMV reactivation vs CNI+MTX/MMF (OR 1.26 [1.07–1.47]). In C2, the point estimate is directionally protective (OR 0.92 [0.73–1.15]), but the CrI crosses null. The qualitative direction reversal reported in the pre-Block-9 analysis (C2 OR 0.77 [0.60–0.99]) is attenuated.

Sensitivity: expanded arm inclusion as a confirmatory test
The C2 sensitivity analysis provides a stronger test of the depletion hierarchy than the primary analysis alone. By reclassifying PTCy+ATG combination arms as “PTCy-side,” the sensitivity asks: what happens to the treatment effect when the PTCy arm also carries ATG-mediated T-cell depletion?
The depletion hierarchy makes three predictions, all confirmed:

Figure 3: C2 primary vs sensitivity (expanded arm inclusion). CMV converges to null when PTCy arms also use ATG — confirming that infection risk tracks depletion depth. OS strengthens; aGVHD attenuates.











ImportantThe Sensitivity Pattern Confirms the Hierarchy




CMV converges to null (primary OR 0.92 → sensitivity 1). When PTCy arms also use ATG, both sides of the comparison have deep T-cell depletion. CMV rates equalise — exactly as the hierarchy predicts. If the C1 CMV excess were an intrinsic PTCy property (rather than a relative depletion effect), adding ATG to the PTCy arm should have made things worse, not better.
aGVHD attenuates (primary 0.58 → sensitivity 0.78). Adding ATG to the PTCy arm reduces the differential in alloreactive T-cell depletion between arms, narrowing the GVHD advantage. This is the GVHD-pathway analogue of the CMV convergence.
OS strengthens (primary 0.81 → sensitivity 0.74). PTCy+ATG combinations appear to improve survival more than ATG alone, possibly through redundant GVHD suppression from both agents. This may explain why the aGVHD and CMV effects attenuate (both arms are deeply immunosuppressed) while survival still improves.





Synthesis
The primary C2 CMV estimate alone no longer demonstrates a statistically credible direction reversal. However, the three-way pattern across the primary and sensitivity analyses — C1 harmful, C2-primary near-null, C2-sensitivity null — traces a dose–response curve along the depletion axis. The framework is better supported by this graded pattern than it was by the pre-Block-9 binary reversal, even though the individual C2 CMV CrI is wider.


Comparator ATG use moderates the C1 CMV effect
A further test of the depletion hierarchy exists within the C1 data itself. Although C1 comparator arms are defined as “CNI+MTX/MMF,” many also received ATG — and when they did, the CMV effect changes direction.

Figure 4: C1 CMV effect stratified by comparator-arm ATG use. When the comparator also uses ATG (i.e. both arms deplete T cells), the CMV excess vanishes — the same convergence seen in the C2 sensitivity analysis.





When the comparator arm uses ATG (k = 12), the pooled OR is 1.05 — essentially null, identical to the C2 pattern. When the comparator has no ATG (k = 7), the OR is 1.25, showing a PTCy-associated CMV excess. The moderator test is borderline (p = 0.501, R² = 1%).
This is the depletion hierarchy operating within a single comparison. The CMV excess attributed to PTCy is not an intrinsic PTCy effect — it is a relative effect that depends on how much T-cell depletion the comparator carries. This pattern was independently confirmed in the C2 expanded-arm sensitivity analysis (above), where adding ATG to the PTCy arm similarly converged CMV toward null.


CMV and donor/recipient serostatus
The depletion hierarchy predicts that PTCy should increase CMV reactivation most when CMV-specific T-cell reconstitution matters most — i.e., when the recipient carries latent virus (R+). We assessed this in two ways.
Meta-regression. Neither recipient seropositivity (k = 11, p = 0.72) nor D+/R+ prevalence (k = 8, p = 0.43) significantly moderated the PTCy effect on CMV when used as study-level ecological covariates. Both analyses were severely underpowered (only 8–11 of 22 C1 CMV studies report arm-level serostatus data).

The D−/R+ stratum is the only one where PTCy did not increase CMV risk. In this configuration, the recipient carries CMV-specific memory T cells from prior infection (R+) but the donor does not (D−). Post-transplant immune reconstitution against CMV therefore relies on surviving recipient memory cells. PTCy’s preferential depletion of alloreactive (recently activated) T cells may spare these quiescent, CMV-specific memory cells, whereas CNI-based regimens continuously suppress all T-cell function including memory responses. This is consistent with the mechanistic selectivity of cyclophosphamide for dividing cells.
In contrast, when the donor is seropositive (D+/R+ and D+/R−), the comparator arm benefits from donor-derived CMV-specific T cells during immune reconstitution — a pathway that PTCy disrupts by depleting the incoming donor graft during the early post-transplant window.

All D/R stratum-specific estimates are based on k = 1 study each. The ecological meta-regressions lack power (k = 8–11 with restricted ranges). Testing whether PTCy’s CMV effect genuinely differs by D/R serostatus requires individual patient data (IPD) meta-analysis, where within-study D/R interactions can be estimated without ecological bias.

NoteATG Is Not the Solution



The C2 data — and especially the sensitivity analysis — show that ATG-based regimens carry at least as great a T-cell reconstitution liability as PTCy. Adding ATG to PTCy does not worsen CMV; it merely saturates the depletion effect. The infection costs of PTCy are best understood as a general consequence of T-cell–depleting prophylaxis, not a PTCy-specific limitation.

title: Discussion
text:
Limitations

Observational evidence. All findings derive from retrospective cohort and registry studies. Residual confounding cannot be excluded despite mediation modelling.
Sparse infection data. BSI (k = 6) and IFI (k = 6) are data-poor. Dedicated prospective studies are needed.
Relapse data not analysed. The residual OS benefit (surviving steroid adjustment) is hypothesised to reflect graft-versus-leukaemia preservation, but relapse data were not extracted.
Publication bias. RoBMA (Robust Bayesian Model-Averaging) detected strong evidence of publication bias for C1 OS (BF = 10.9) and C1 aGVHD (BF = 14.1), with moderate evidence for C2 OS (BF = 5.2) and C2 aGVHD (BF = 4.1). After bias adjustment, all model-averaged effects collapsed toward the null (P(effect) < 50% for all 9 outcomes). No meaningful bias was detected for C1 CMV, NRM, BSI, or IFI (BFs < 1). The RoBMA default priors are deliberately skeptical (Normal(0, 1) on log-OR, 50% prior mass on the null), and the prospective/RCT subgroup analysis (below) suggests these estimates may be overly conservative — but the bias signals for OS and aGVHD warrant caution in interpreting effect magnitudes.
Observational dominance and design-associated confounding. Only 14 of 251 studies are RCTs, and very few contribute to the paired analyses (2 RCTs in C1 OS; 0 in any C2 outcome). A prospective-vs-retrospective subgroup analysis of C1 outcomes showed that OS estimates were concordant across designs (prospective OR 0.76 vs retrospective 0.78), while C1 CMV showed a complete direction reversal (prospective OR 0.68 vs retrospective 1.39, p = 0.056). Investigation revealed this reversal is driven by case-mix confounding — all 3 prospective studies used matched donors (0% haplo) and 2/3 had ATG in the comparator arm — rather than reporting bias. This underscores that apparent “study quality” effects in this literature may reflect systematic differences in donor type, conditioning, and comparator regimen rather than methodological rigour per se.
Haplo proportion as effect modifier. Meta-regression identified haplo donor proportion as a significant moderator of the aGVHD treatment effect in both C1 (β = +0.005/%, p = 0.049, R² = 22%) and C2 (β = +0.013/%, p = 0.034, R² = 47%), and of C1 OS (β = +0.005/%, p = 0.003, R² = 26%). PTCy’s advantages over both comparators attenuate as haplo proportion increases, reaching null at ~100% haplo for aGVHD and OS. This is not confounded by conditioning intensity and is mechanistically coherent, but it means the pooled estimates — which average across a range of haplo proportions — may overstate or understate the effect for any specific clinical scenario.
M2 complete-case analysis. Post-Block-9 M2 models use complete-case analysis for steroid adjustment (dropping arms with missing steroid data), differing from the pre-Block-9 mi() imputation approach due to a brms API change.
C2 CMV sensitivity caveats. The expanded-arm sensitivity conflates PTCy+ATG combination arms (which test a different clinical question — whether adding PTCy to ATG changes outcomes) with pure PTCy vs ATG comparisons. The convergence pattern is mechanistically interpretable but should not be taken as evidence that PTCy+ATG combinations are clinically equivalent to ATG alone.

title: GRADE Certainty Assessment
text:
Narrative Summary
Across both comparisons, certainty does not exceed LOW — a predictable consequence of an almost entirely observational evidence base.
The most robust finding is C1 OS (OR 0.79, k = 40, LOW certainty), which has been stable across the pre-Block-9 and post-Block-9 analyses, is consistent across comparators (C2 OR 0.81), and has CrIs that exclude null. C1 aGVHD (OR 0.67, k = 28) is consistent across comparators (C2 OR 0.58, k = 9) and directionally stable, but is downgraded to VERY LOW due to significant funnel asymmetry (Egger p = 0.041). The trim-and-fill adjusted estimate (OR 0.83) crosses null, suggesting the effect size may be inflated by selective reporting of small positive studies. Cross-comparison coherence remains the strongest methodological asset.
The CMV depletion hierarchy is supported not by a single direction reversal but by a three-point gradient across the primary and sensitivity analyses. This gradient pattern carries greater evidential weight than any one estimate. Certainty for the mechanistic conclusion (that CMV risk tracks depletion depth) is LOW when integrating the full pattern.
Infection outcomes remain the principal evidence gap. BSI and IFI carry VERY LOW certainty. Both show substantial discordance between Bayesian and frequentist estimators, and both have extreme heterogeneity. Dedicated prospective studies with standardised endpoint definitions are needed.
C2 NRM is no longer gradeable. Arm classification corrections reduced k to 2. The steroid mediation pattern observed in C1 NRM (OR 0.88 → M2 OR 0.90) remains the best available evidence for the GVHD→steroid→NRM causal chain.






TipPost-Block-9 GRADE Changes




C2 NRM: removed (k = 2 after arm reclassification)
C2 BSI: removed (k = 3 Mantel-Haenszel was not formally gradeable)
C2 CMV: still VERY LOW; reasoning revised from “direction reversal” to “gradient pattern”
C1 IFI: k decreased (8 → 6), but CrI now excludes null; τ = 1.64 warrants extreme caution
All other outcomes: certainty unchanged

Comparison 2: Haplo Proportion as Effect Modifier
The proportion of haploidentical donors in the PTCy arm varies substantially across C2 studies (0–100%). We tested whether this modifies the PTCy-vs-ATG treatment effect via frequentist meta-regression with haplo_pct as a continuous moderator.


Show code
plot_metareg <- function(es_df, fit, outcome_label) {
  df <- data.frame(
    haplo_pct = es_df$haplo_pct,
    or = exp(es_df$yi),
    wi = 1 / es_df$vi
  )

  newdat <- data.frame(haplo_pct = seq(0, 100, 1))

    geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = jama_grey) +
    geom_ribbon(data = pred_df, aes(y = or, ymin = lo, ymax = hi),

M1 (Direct effect): OR 0.77 (95% CrI 0.71–0.83), P(OR < 1) = 100%, τ = 0.59. The posterior is entirely below the null, indicating a consistent mortality reduction with PTCy.
M2 (Steroid-adjusted): Adjusting for arm-level systemic steroid exposure attenuated the OR from 0.77 to 0.83 (95% CrI 0.75–0.92), a 29% reduction in the log-OR. The residual benefit after adjustment indicates GVHD mediation does not fully explain the OS advantage.

title: Risk of Bias
text:
Risk of bias (ROB) was assessed using the ROBINS-I tool (Risk Of Bias In Non-randomised Studies – of Interventions), adapted for comparative observational studies in transplant medicine. Seven domains were evaluated:

Confounding — baseline differences between PTCy and comparator arms
Selection — participant selection into study or comparison group
Classification — misclassification of the intervention (GVHD prophylaxis)
Deviations — departures from intended interventions
Missing data — incomplete outcome data
Measurement — outcome measurement bias
Reporting — selective reporting of outcomes

Each domain was rated as Low, Moderate, Serious, or Critical risk of bias.

title: Risk of Bias
Risk of Bias
text:
Key ROB Considerations by Outcome

Overall Survival







Concern
Assessment




Confounding
Moderate–Serious. PTCy arms enriched for haploidentical donors (younger, fitter recipients). M2 steroid adjustment partially addresses GVHD-mediated confounding but cannot eliminate all baseline imbalances.


Selection
Moderate. Registry-based studies reduce individual selection bias but introduce centre-level selection.


Measurement
Low. OS is an objective endpoint not subject to ascertainment bias.





CMV Reactivation







Concern
Assessment




Confounding
Serious. Donor CMV serostatus, letermovir prophylaxis, and monitoring intensity vary by arm and era.


Measurement
Moderate. CMV monitoring frequency may differ between PTCy and comparator arms (awareness bias). More intensive surveillance in PTCy arms could inflate ascertainment.


Reporting
Low. CMV reactivation is routinely reported in transplant cohorts.





BSI







Concern
Assessment




Missing data
Very serious (C1). 7 of 13 eligible studies had non-reported event counts, creating substantial attrition bias.


Classification
Moderate (C2). Outcome definitions varied (any positive culture vs ICU/fatal only).


Confounding
Serious (C2). Donor-type imbalance in the dominant study (Meyer 2025).





IFI







Concern
Assessment




Confounding
Serious. Antifungal prophylaxis regimens are heterogeneous and non-randomly distributed. PTCy centres disproportionately use prolonged mold-active azole prophylaxis.


Measurement
Moderate. IFI diagnosis requires invasive procedures (bronchoscopy/biopsy); investigation intensity may differ between arms.

title: Risk of Bias
text:
Impact on Interpretation
Risk of bias is a consistent limitation across all outcomes, reflecting the almost exclusively observational evidence base. The mediation models (M2, M3) partially address confounding by adjusting for GVHD-driven steroid exposure, but residual confounding from baseline characteristics (age, disease risk, donor type, conditioning intensity) cannot be excluded.
The most robust findings are those where:

The effect survives covariate adjustment (OS, CMV in C1)
The direction is consistent across comparators with different confounding structures (OS, aGVHD)
Plausible bias would oppose rather than inflate the observed effect (aGVHD)
